web_title: 3. Unit Economics, ₹100 Waterfall & Working Capital Mechanics
book_title: Chapter 3: Follow the Cash — The ₹100 Waterfall, Acceptances & Working Capital
question: Out of every ₹100 of Apar's FY26 revenue, how much survives to operating profit, net profit, and free cash flow—and how do LC acceptances and DDP transit shape cash conversion?

epigraph.quote: Revenue is vanity, EBITDA is sanity, but in metal-heavy manufacturing, cash conversion after working capital and acceptances interest is reality.
epigraph.author: Industrial Forensic Principle

web_blocks.html: To strip out metal-price swings and show true unit economics, every FY26 line item is scaled to ₹100.00 of sales (₹22,902 crore) below [1][4]. One key accounting point stands out. Screener reports FY26 Operating Profit at ₹1,922 crore (8.39% margin) after ₹20,980 crore of operating costs [1]. By contrast, Apar's investor deck reports EBITDA post open-period forex at ₹2,067 crore (9.03%) [3]. Both numbers tie cleanly to the same audited ₹977 crore net profit (4.27% PAT margin) and ₹968 crore operating cash flow [1][4].

notes.revenue: Audited FY26 consolidated revenue from operations: ₹22,902 Cr (+23.3% YoY) [1][4].
notes.cogs: BSE FY26 cost of materials consumed (₹18,694.25 Cr) + stock-in-trade (₹103.42 Cr) - inventory change (₹706.82 Cr) = ₹18,090.85 Cr (~79.0% of sales) [4].
notes.employee_cost: BSE FY26 audited employee benefits expense: ₹427.87 Cr (1.87% of sales) [4].
notes.other_opex: Screener total expenses (₹20,980 Cr) less COGS (₹18,091 Cr) and payroll (₹428 Cr); BSE raw other expenses were ₹2,507.47 Cr before ₹46 Cr operating/forex reclassification [1][4].
notes.ebitda: Screener Operating Profit: ₹1,922 Cr (8.39% of sales); company presentation reports ₹2,067 Cr post open-period forex [1][3].
notes.da: Audited FY26 depreciation & amortization: ₹161 Cr (0.70% of sales) — low asset intensity relative to turnover [1].
notes.interest: Audited FY26 finance costs: ₹474 Cr (2.07% of sales), dominated by LC acceptances and working-capital interest [1][10].
notes.other_income: Audited FY26 other income: ₹24 Cr (0.10% of sales) [1].
notes.pbt: Audited FY26 profit before tax: ₹1,310 Cr (5.72% of sales; ₹1 Cr rounding on line items) [1].
notes.tax: Audited FY26 tax expense: ₹333 Cr (25.4% effective tax rate) [1].
notes.pat: Audited FY26 net profit: ₹977 Cr (4.27% PAT margin) [1][3].
notes.working_capital: Net working-capital absorption & non-cash adjustments bridging PAT + D&A (₹1,138 Cr) to CFO (₹968 Cr) [1].
notes.cfo: Audited FY26 cash flow from operations: ₹968 Cr (70% CFO/EBITDA pre-tax conversion) [1].
notes.capex: FY26 fixed-asset capex ~₹733–737 Cr (Screener CFO ₹968 Cr less FCF ₹235 Cr) [1][20].
notes.fcf: Audited FY26 free cash flow: ₹235 Cr (1.03% of sales) during heavy capacity expansion [1].

web_blocks.caption: APARINDS: Audited FY26 ₹100 Revenue-to-Free-Cash-Flow Waterfall (₹22,902 Cr)
web_blocks.takeaway: Out of every ₹100 of FY26 sales, ₹79.00 goes to raw materials (aluminium, copper, base oil), leaving ₹8.39 in operating EBITDA; ₹2.07 is consumed by finance costs (mostly LC acceptances), yielding ₹4.27 in net profit, ₹4.23 in operating cash flow, and ₹1.03 in free cash flow after ₹3.20 of growth capex.

web_blocks.html: The waterfall highlights the core tension in Apar's model. On fixed assets alone, Apar is very capital-light. FY26 Depreciation was just ₹161 crore (0.70% of sales) [1]. Fixed Assets plus CWIP stood at ₹2,257 crore in March 2026 on ₹22,902 crore of sales—over 10x fixed-asset turnover [1]. Even with CWIP rising to ₹903 crore in September 2026 (Fixed Assets ₹1,813 crore), plant intensity stays low relative to output [1]. That drives Apar's strong 31.8% headline ROCE [1]. Yet metal conversion needs heavy working capital. Other Assets—mainly stock and trade receivables—hit ₹11,399 crore in March 2026 and ₹13,275 crore in September 2026 [1].

In the past, Apar funded that ₹11,000+ crore asset pool via ₹3,946 crore (FY24) to ₹4,079 crore (FY25) of short-term Letter of Credit (LC) acceptances [10]. CARE Ratings' September 2026 credit rationale revealed that FY26 working-capital requirements jumped to ₹8,520 crore (~37% of operating income; ₹5,334 crore debtors + ₹3,186 crore inventory), pushing average non-fund-based bank limit utilization to ~88% for the 12 months ended May 2026 (up from ~75% YoY) with pre-QIP overall gearing (including LC acceptances) at 1.11x and TOL/TNW at 1.54x [22]. That held Days Payable at 137–138 days (against 85 Debtor Days + 84 Inventory Days = 39–43 Working Capital Days), while the hidden cost hit the P&L as ₹443–₹474 crore of yearly interest—near 25% of FY26 Operating Profit [1][10]. Quarterly interest stayed high at ₹123 crore in Q1 FY27 and ₹138 crore in Q2 FY27 (₹504 crore TTM) before full QIP deployment [1].

web_blocks.caption: Working Capital & Cash Conversion Cycle Evolution (FY21–FY26)
web_blocks.takeaway: As Days Payable compressed from 231 days (FY21) to 138 days (FY26), Working Capital Days rose from 18–27 days to 39–50 days, making permanent equity funding essential.

web_blocks.title: Q2 FY27 FORENSIC WATCH: ₹800 CRORE IN US DDP TRANSIT
paragraphs: Exporting to the United States on Delivered Duty Paid (DDP) terms shifts ocean-transit time onto Apar's balance sheet. On the Q2 FY27 earnings call (October 29, 2026), management disclosed that roughly ₹800 crore worth of conductors and cables shipped to U.S. customers (including over ₹440 crore of cables alone—nearly 20% of quarterly cable sales value) remained in transit at quarter-end due to container and shipping bottlenecks, deferring revenue recognition into Q3 FY27 [12][13][21].
Investors must track Working Capital Days (43 days in FY26, up from 18 days in FY23) and CFO/EBITDA conversion (70% in FY26 vs 97% in FY25) as U.S. DDP shipments scale [1][12].

web_blocks.title: 3.3 How the August 2026 QIP Reshapes Unit Economics

web_blocks.html: The ₹2,500 crore QIP in August 2026 directly cuts the interest drag in Apar's ₹100 waterfall [10][15]. Crucially, CARE Ratings notes that ₹1,875 crore (75%) of QIP proceeds is explicitly earmarked for working capital to partly replace short-term LC acceptances and relieve the 88% pre-QIP non-fund-based bank limit saturation [22]. Alongside internal accruals funding the ₹1,500 crore FY27 domestic capex program, retiring costly acceptances can lower finance costs from the ₹474–₹504 crore TTM run rate [1][10][19][22]. A ₹150–₹200 crore drop in yearly interest flows straight to pre-tax profit, cushioning earnings as conductor and oil margins normalize while pushing TOL/TNW below 1.0x [10][11][22].

book_paragraphs: Whenever you and I look at a ₹22,902 crore manufacturing business, headline sales can hypnotize us [1]. Copper and aluminium prices move up, revenue jumps 23%, and everyone celebrates. The only way to stay grounded is to shrink the entire FY26 income and cash-flow statement down to a single ₹100 bill and watch where every rupee goes [1][4].

Out of ₹100 of Apar's FY26 revenue, ₹79.00 walks right back out the door to pay for raw aluminium, copper, and base oils [4]. Only ₹1.87 goes to employee payroll (₹427.87 crore across the entire global workforce), and ₹10.74 covers other operating overhead, leaving ₹8.39 of Screener Operating Profit—or ₹9.03 if you use management's post-forex EBITDA presentation of ₹2,067 crore [1][3][4]. Depreciation is tiny—just ₹0.70 per ₹100 of sales (₹161 crore)—because Apar turns its factories more than ten times over on revenue [1]. That asset-light manufacturing footprint is the engine behind its 31.8% Return on Capital Employed [1].

Now look at the leak right below Operating EBIT: ₹2.07 out of every ₹100 of sales—₹474 crore in absolute cash—vanished into finance costs in FY26, rising to ₹504 crore on a trailing twelve-month basis through September 2026 [1]. For a company carrying only ₹956 crore of formal balance-sheet borrowings in March 2026, paying ₹474 crore in interest looks bizarre until you open CARE Ratings' September 2026 credit rationale [1][10][22]. FY26 working-capital requirements jumped to ₹8,520 crore (~37% of operating income: ₹5,334 crore receivables plus ₹3,186 crore inventory), funded largely through LC-backed acceptances where average non-fund-based bank limit utilization climbed to ~88% (up from ~75% YoY) and pre-QIP gearing including acceptances stood at 1.11x (TOL/TNW 1.54x) [10][22]. Suppliers were financing Apar's inventory for 138 days, and bank acceptance fees ate a quarter of operating profit [1][10].

After ₹333 crore of taxes (₹1.45 per ₹100, a clean 25.4% rate), Apar kept ₹4.27 of net profit per ₹100 of sales (₹977 crore total) and converted virtually all of it into ₹4.23 of operating cash flow (₹968 crore, or 70% pre-tax CFO/EBITDA conversion) [1]. Subtract ₹3.20 per ₹100 for growth capex (₹733–₹737 crore), and ₹1.03 per ₹100 survived as true Free Cash Flow (₹235 crore) [1][20]. That is healthy—especially compared to FY24 when rapid expansion drove CFO negative (-₹283 crore)—but it also shows why working capital is the steering wheel of this enterprise [1].

Watch what happens when Apar ships to the United States on Delivered Duty Paid (DDP) terms [12]. In Q2 FY27 alone, ₹800 crore of finished conductors and cables—including over ₹440 crore of cables alone—sat on ships in transit at quarter-end, tying up cash and delaying revenue recognition [12][13][21]. Meanwhile, Working Capital Days climbed from 18 days in FY23 to 43 days in FY26 as Days Payable tightened from 172 to 138 days [1]. That is precisely why management earmarked ₹1,875 crore (75%) of the August 2026 ₹2,500 crore QIP specifically for working capital [22]: swapping expensive LC acceptances for permanent equity relieves the 88% bank-limit squeeze and shrinks that ₹2.07 interest leak while funding ₹1,500 crore of fresh FY27 capex [10][19][22].

book_subsections.title: The Hidden Cost of Negative Working Capital
paragraphs: Textbooks teach us that negative or low working capital is always free financing. Apar's P&L proves the nuance: when your Days Payable of 138 days relies on interest-bearing LC acceptances rather than interest-free trade credit, the 'free' float actually shows up inside finance costs [1][10].

As QIP proceeds retire those acceptances and push TOL/TNW below 1.0x [10][22], you and I should watch whether interest expense as a percentage of sales finally breaks below 1.5% over the next four quarters—a clean, measurable test of balance-sheet improvement.

book_subsections.title: Why Asset Turnover Explains the 32% ROCE
paragraphs: Notice the contrast inside Apar's balance sheet: Fixed Assets plus CWIP stood at just ₹2,257 crore at March 2026, while Other Assets (inventories, receivables, cash) stood at ₹11,399 crore [1]. Apar does not need massive blast furnaces; it needs working-capital velocity.
As long as Debtor Days stay near 80–85 days and Inventory Days near 82–85 days [1], the business generates elite returns on invested capital—even during a ₹1,500 crore capex cycle [19].

book_subsections.title: Walking the ₹100 Revenue-to-Free-Cash-Flow Waterfall
paragraphs: Let us trace every single rupee of Apar Industries' audited FY26 consolidated revenue from the top line down to free cash flow. Out of every ₹100 of FY26 sales (₹22,902 Cr total), raw materials—primarily aluminium rod, copper rod, and naphthenic/paraffinic base oils—consume ₹79.00 (₹18,091 Cr) [1][4]. That single number tells you why Apar is fundamentally a conversion-margin business rather than a software-margin business: management cannot control whether LME aluminium is at $2,400 or $2,800 per metric ton, so it relies on back-to-back hedging and contractual price-variation clauses to pass metal swings through to utilities and EPC customers.

Once you subtract employee costs (₹1.87 per ₹100, or ₹428 Cr) and other manufacturing, freight, and selling expenses (₹10.74 per ₹100, or ₹2,461 Cr), Apar retains ₹8.39 of Screener operating EBITDA per ₹100 of revenue (₹1,922 Cr consolidated operating profit) [1][4]. Depreciation takes ₹0.70 (₹161 Cr), while finance costs—driven heavily by letter-of-credit acceptances and working-capital interest—consume ₹2.07 per ₹100 (₹474 Cr). After adding ₹0.10 of other income (₹24 Cr) and paying ₹1.45 in taxes (₹333 Cr), Apar brings home ₹4.27 of net profit per ₹100 of sales (₹977 Cr FY26 PAT) [1].

Now watch what happens on the cash flow statement, because this is where industrial compounders prove their discipline. In FY26, Apar generated ₹4.23 of Cash Flow from Operations (₹968 Cr) per ₹100 of sales—nearly 100% of accounting net profit—even while funding rapid 23.3% top-line growth [1]. After reinvesting ₹3.20 per ₹100 into growth capital expenditure (₹733–₹737 Cr across Silvassa, Jharsuguda, Khatalwada, and Umbergaon), Apar still produced ₹1.03 of genuine Free Cash Flow (₹235 Cr) per ₹100 of revenue [1][20]. That discipline explains why the balance sheet absorbed multi-year growth before management proactively fortified equity via the August 2026 QIP.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: In commodity-converting industrials, fixed-asset turnover gets the headlines, but working-capital financing decides who keeps the profit. Apar's ₹100 waterfall shows an 8.4% operating business that gave away a quarter of its profit to acceptance interest—and just raised ₹2,500 crore to plug that leak.
